lede: A café tells you three things about its prices without telling you a single price. Each sentence is an equation waiting to be written, and once all three are on the page the solving is the part you already know. The marks are almost all in the writing down.
can: Define three letters with their units, then turn one sentence into one equation
Translate a dearer-by and a per-cent-greater comparison without losing a mark to either
Derive a printed equation forwards, then scale your answer back into the context's units

md:
A café tells you three things about its prices without telling you a single price.
Each sentence is an equation waiting to be written. Once the three are on the page the solving is the part you already know, and almost all the marks sit in the writing down.

answer: A definition of each letter, with its unit
explain: The unit is the part that does the work. Choosing pounds here means 70p is written as $0.7$ everywhere, and a whole class of slips never happens.

md:
Work through the question one sentence at a time and write the equation that sentence gives before reading the next.
A **total** ("three coffees and two scones cost ...") becomes a sum with the counts as coefficients. A **comparison** ("dearer than", "twice as many") becomes an equation in two letters. Both are one line each, and both are worth marks on their own.

prompt: An order of $3$ scones, $1$ coffee and $1$ bowl of soup costs $£9.45$. Write that as an equation.
explain: Each count multiplies its own letter, and a count of one is written as the bare letter: $3x + y + z = 9.45$. Leaving out a letter whose count is one is the omission examiners report most.

md:
"70p dearer" is a fixed amount, so it is added: $y = x + 0.7$.
"50% greater" is a share of something else, so it multiplies: $z = 1.5y$.
Both also need the right item on its own. Whichever the sentence calls dearer is the letter that stands alone.

title: Why a percentage can never be added
md:
A percentage has no size until you say what it is a percentage of. 50% of a coffee at £2.10 is £1.05; 50% of something else is something else again.
So it has to multiply the letter it refers to. Written as a number on its own it stops depending on that letter.

prompt: A bowl of soup costs $50$% more than a coffee. Which equation says that?
explain: A rise of $50$% multiplies by $1.5$, and the soup is the dearer item so its letter stands alone. The middle option prices the soup at $£52.10$.

alt: Three boxes, one for each café order, each showing the three prices substituted in and the left-hand side agreeing with the bill on the right.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 560 176' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The three café prices substituted back into the order equation'><title>The three café prices substituted back into the order equation</title><rect x='20' y='22' width='520' height='30' rx='5' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.1'/><text x='32' y='42' font-family='inherit' font-size='13' fill='currentColor'>(1)  2(1.4) + 3(2.1) + 1(3.15) = 12.25</text><text x='530' y='42' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='end'>agrees</text><rect x='20' y='68' width='520' height='30' rx='5' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.1'/><text x='32' y='88' font-family='inherit' font-size='13' fill='currentColor'>(2)  1(1.4) + 2(2.1) + 2(3.15) = 11.9</text><text x='530' y='88' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='end'>agrees</text><rect x='20' y='114' width='520' height='30' rx='5' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.1'/><text x='32' y='134' font-family='inherit' font-size='13' fill='currentColor'>(3)  3(1.4) + 1(2.1) + 1(3.15) = 9.45</text><text x='530' y='134' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='end'>agrees</text><text x='280' y='172' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>Two equations built the answer, so the third is the real test</text></svg>
caption: Scone $£1.40$, coffee $£2.10$, soup $£3.15$, checked in all three orders.

md:
**The three sentences.** $(1)$ $y = x + 0.7$, $(2)$ $z = 1.5y$, $(3)$ $2x + 3y + z = 12.25$.
**Substitute, because $(1)$ and $(2)$ offer it.** Putting both into $(3)$ leaves $6.5x + 3.15 = 12.25$, so $x = 1.4$.
**Back through the comparisons.** $y = 2.1$ and $z = 3.15$.
**Answer in the café's words.** A scone is $£1.40$, a coffee $£2.10$ and a bowl of soup $£3.15$.

title: Simultaneous Equations with Three Unknowns in a Context - Corbettmaths
why: The same route on a different context, at a slower pace. Watch how long is spent on the sentences before any solving starts.

prompt: In that solution, a coffee came out at $£2.10$. Using $(2)$, what is the price of a bowl of soup, in pounds?
explain: $1.5 \times 2.1 = 3.15$. The comparisons are the cheapest equations to substitute back into, so use them rather than the long order equation.

md:
A "show that" prints the equation you have to arrive at. The marks are for the arriving, so the working runs forwards: from the information, to an equation of your own, to the printed one.
Compare one of your coefficients with the printed one to find the factor. If the printed number is smaller you divide; the same factor then has to work on every term, the right-hand side included.

title: What the reports say about this part
md: Candidates who started at the printed equation and checked that the information fitted it earned nothing, however neat the page. In another series the commonest error was multiplying where the step was a division.

prompt: Your equation is $12x + 8y + 6z = 78$ and the printed form is $6x + 4y + 3z = 39$. What do you divide every term by?
explain: $12 \div 2 = 6$, and the same factor takes $78$ to $39$. If a factor does not work on all four numbers, the line above it is wrong.

md:
Money questions come in two units and the question rarely uses one of them throughout. Choose the one that keeps your coefficients whole, write it into the definitions, and convert everything else to match.
A jar of coins is easiest in pence. A firm's profits are usually given in thousands, and then the right-hand side is in thousands too, so £78000 is written as $78$.

prompt: The letters are profits in thousands of pounds and the solving gives $x = 2$. What is the profit in pounds?
explain: Multiply by $1000$: $2 \times 1000 = 2000$. This is the step the reports say goes missing after solving that was otherwise faultless.

md:
The same method fits a curve. A point on $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ fixes $x$ and $y$, so substituting them leaves a linear equation in the three coefficients.
Three points give three such equations, and they are solved exactly like any other system. Work out $x^2$ as you substitute, so the coefficient of $a$ is a number: at $x = 2$ the first term is $4a$, not $2a$.

prompt: The curve passes through $(3, 28)$. Write the equation that point gives.
explain: $x = 3$ makes $x^2 = 9$, so the equation is $9a + 3b + c = 28$.

text: 7 When the answer cannot be true

md:
Read your three values as the things they stand for before you write them on the answer line. A negative age, a negative number of coins, a scone dearer than a three-course meal: each of those is a message.
The message is almost always about the forming rather than the solving, because the elimination is usually faithful to whatever equations it was given. Go back to the sentence, not to the arithmetic.

prompt: Your solving gives an age of $-2$ years. What do you do?
options: Change the sign to make it sensible
Write it down and move on
explain: The elimination is usually sound, so the fault is earlier. Here it is a comparison written the wrong way round: $(2)$ should read $x - y = 5$.

md:
Define three letters with their units before writing any algebra.
Turn a total, a comparison and a percentage comparison each into one equation.
Derive a printed equation forwards and reach it by dividing the whole equation.
Keep one unit throughout, and scale the answer back into the unit the question asked for.
Read the three values as the things they stand for, and act on an impossible one.

prompt: Before the reference panel, one check on the recap. What goes on the page first?
options: A definition of each letter, with its unit
The elimination you plan to use
answer: A definition of each letter, with its unit
explain: The unit decides what every later number means, and the definitions are the cheapest marks in the question.

md: This is the long question near the end of the paper. The short parts each form or derive one equation and are marked on their own, so a wrong first equation does not stop the second earning. The first mark is for one equation that matches its sentence; the last is for the context step after the solving. If you are stuck, form the equations you can see.
